text: Costco Wholesale Corporation and its subsidiaries (Costco or the Company) began operations in 1983 in Seattle, Washington. The Company operates membership warehouses in the United States, Puerto Rico, Canada, the United Kingdom, Mexico, Japan, Korea, Australia, Spain, France, Iceland, China, and through a majority-owned subsidiary in Taiwan. As of August 29, 2021, Costco operated 815 warehouses worldwide, 795 as of August 30, 2020, and 782 as of September 1, 2019. The Company operates e-commerce websites in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, the U.K., Korea, Taiwan, Japan, and Australia. Its common stock trades on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the symbol “COST.” The Company reports on a 52/53-week fiscal year consisting of thirteen four-week periods, ending on the Sunday nearest the end of August. The first three quarters consist of three periods each, and the fourth quarter consists of four periods (five weeks in a 53-week year). The winter holiday season has a material seasonal impact, with increased net sales and earnings. References to 2021, 2020, and 2019 pertain to the 52-week fiscal years ended August 29, 2021, August 30, 2020, and September 1, 2019, respectively. Costco operates membership warehouses and e-commerce websites based on the concept of offering members low prices on a limited selection of nationally-branded and private-label products across a wide range of categories, resulting in high sales volumes and rapid inventory turnover. This is combined with volume purchasing, efficient distribution, and reduced handling in no-frills, self-service warehouse facilities, enabling profitable operations with significantly lower gross margins than most retailers. The Company generally sells inventory before paying for it, taking advantage of early payment discounts. Most merchandise is purchased directly from manufacturers and routed to cross-docking consolidation points (depots) or directly to warehouses. Depots receive large shipments and quickly ship goods to warehouses, creating freight volume and handling efficiencies that reduce distribution costs. For e-commerce, merchandise is shipped through depots, logistics operations for big and bulky items, and via drop-ship or other supplier delivery arrangements. The average warehouse space is approximately 146,000 square feet, with newer units slightly larger. Floor plans are designed for economy and efficiency in selling space, merchandise handling, and inventory control. Warehouses are not elaborate, as shoppers are primarily attracted by merchandise quality and low prices, and the Company strictly controls entrances and exits, resulting in inventory losses (shrinkage) well below typical retail levels. Warehouses operate on a seven-day, 70-hour week, with gasoline operations having extended hours. Due to shorter operating hours and operational efficiencies, labor costs are lower relative to sales volume. Merchandise is stored on racks above the sales floor and displayed on pallets with large quantities, reducing labor needs. In general, with country variations, warehouses accept certain credit cards, including Costco co-branded cards, debit cards, cash, checks, co-brand cardholder rebates, Executive member 2% reward certificates, and the Company’s proprietary stored-value card (shop card). The Company’s strategy is to provide members with a broad range of high-quality merchandise at prices believed to be consistently lower than elsewhere, limiting most items to fast-selling models, sizes, and colors. It carries less than 4,000 active stock keeping units (SKUs) per warehouse in its core business, significantly fewer than other broadline retailers, and averages between 9,000 and 11,000 SKUs online, some of which are also available in warehouses. Many consumable products are offered only in case, carton, or multiple-pack quantities. In line with member satisfaction, the Company generally accepts returns of merchandise, with a 90-day return policy for electronics and free technical support and extended warranties provided. Additional third-party warranty coverage is available on certain electronic items. Core merchandise categories include Foods and Sundries (including sundries, dry grocery, candy, cooler, freezer, deli, liquor, and tobacco), Non-Foods (including major appliances, electronics, health and beauty aids, hardware, garden and patio, sporting goods, tires, toys and seasonal, office supplies, automotive care, postage, tickets, apparel, small appliances, furniture, domestics, housewares, special order kiosk, and jewelry), and Fresh Foods (including meat, produce, service deli, and bakery). Warehouse ancillary businesses include gasoline, pharmacy, optical, food court, hearing aids, and tire installation, operating primarily within or next to warehouses to encourage more frequent shopping. The number of gas stations varies by country, and there is no gasoline business in Korea or China. At the end of 2021, Costco operated 636 gas stations, with gasoline net sales representing approximately 9% of total net sales in 2021. Other businesses include e-commerce, business centers, travel, and other services. E-commerce net sales represented approximately 7% of total net sales in 2021, excluding other online services such as business delivery, travel, same-day grocery, and other offerings. Business centers offer items tailored for food services, convenience stores, and offices, with walk-in shopping and deliveries, and are included in the total warehouse count. Costco Travel offers vacation packages, hotels, cruises, and other travel products exclusively for members in the U.S., Canada, and the U.K. The Company has direct buying relationships with many brand-name producers and does not rely on any single supplier. The COVID-19 pandemic caused unprecedented supply constraints, including disruptions and delays affecting product availability, and the Company seeks alternative sources when supply is unavailable. It also purchases and manufactures private-label merchandise when quality and member demand are high and the value to members is significant. Financial information for segments and geographic areas is included in Note 12 to the consolidated financial statements in Item 8. Membership allows access to all warehouses and websites. Gold Star memberships are available to individuals; Business memberships are limited to businesses, including individuals with a business license, retail sales license, or comparable document. Business members can add additional cardholders (affiliates), with the same annual fee, but affiliates are not available for Gold Star members. The annual membership fee is $60 in the U.S. and Canada and varies in other countries. All paid memberships include a free household card. The member renewal rate was 91% in the U.S. and Canada and 89% worldwide at the end of 2021, with most renewals occurring within six months of the renewal date. The renewal rate is a trailing calculation covering renewals from seven to eighteen months prior to the reporting date. Membership counts include active memberships and those that have not renewed within the prior 12 months. In 2020, the Company standardized its membership count methodology globally to match the U.S. and Canada, adding approximately 2.0 million total cardholders, of which 1.3 million were paid members, without impacting 2019. Membership fee income and renewal rate calculations were unaffected. Membership breakdowns (in thousands) are as follows: 2021: Gold Star 50,200, Business (including affiliates) 11,500, Total paid members 61,700, Household cards 49,900, Total cardholders 111,600; 2020: Gold Star 46,800, Business (including affiliates) 11,300, Total paid members 58,100, Household cards 47,400, Total cardholders 105,500; 2019: Gold Star 42,900, Business (including affiliates) 11,000, Total paid members 53,900, Household cards 44,600, Total cardholders 98,500. Paid cardholders (excluding affiliates) are eligible to upgrade to an Executive membership in the U.S. and Canada for an additional annual fee of $60, and Executive memberships are also available in Mexico, the U.K., Japan, Korea, and Taiwan, with varying annual fees. Executive members earn a 2% reward on qualified purchases (up to a maximum of $1,000 per year), redeemable only at Costco warehouses. The program also offers (except in Mexico and Korea) access to additional savings and benefits on services such as auto and home insurance, the Costco auto purchase program, and check printing, provided by third parties and varying by state and country. At the end of 2021, Executive members totaled 25.6 million, representing 55% of paid members (excluding affiliates) in the U.S. and Canada and 17% of paid members (excluding affiliates) in Other International operations. Executive members generally shop more frequently and spend more than other members. The Company’s Code of Ethics requires that it “Take Care of Our Employees,” which is fundamental to fulfilling its obligation to “Take Care of Our Members.”

Executive membership is available in the U.S. and Canada for an additional annual fee of $60, and is also offered in Mexico, the U.K., Japan, Korea, and Taiwan, with varying annual fees for each country. Executive members receive a 2% reward on qualified purchases, with a maximum annual reward of $1,000, which can only be redeemed at Costco warehouses. In addition to the reward, members in countries other than Mexico and Korea gain access to additional savings and benefits on various business and consumer services, such as auto and home insurance, the Costco auto purchase program, and check printing, which are provided by third parties and vary by state and country. At the end of 2021, executive members totaled 25.6 million, representing 55% of paid members (excluding affiliates) in the U.S. and Canada and 17% of paid members (excluding affiliates) in Other International operations. Executive members generally shop more frequently and spend more than other members. Costco employs 288,000 employees worldwide at the end of 2021, with approximately 95% working in membership warehouses and distribution channels and about 17,000 represented by unions; seasonal employees are used during peak periods. The employee breakdown by segment in 2021 is: United States (192,000), Canada (47,000), Other International (49,000), totaling 288,000. Costco believes its warehouses are among the most productive in retail due to employee commitment and efficiency, and aims to provide careers, not just employment, through competitive compensation and benefits, internal promotion, and maintaining at least a 50% full-time employee ratio. In 2021, the U.S. employee retention rate for those with at least one year of service was above 90%. The company’s commitment to “Take Care of Our Employees” underpins its approach to diversity, equity, and inclusion, including in 2021 adding manager training on race, bias, and equity and increasing visibility of employee demographics. In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, Costco began providing premium pay to most hourly employees in March 2020, continuing through February 2021, with a portion permanently built into U.S. hourly wage scales, and introduced additional paid time off in fall 2020 for child care and schooling needs through the 2021 school year. The company closely monitors the evolving global impact of COVID-19 and complies with public health guidance. Costco competes globally with retailers such as Walmart, Target, Kroger, Amazon, Sam’s Club, BJ’s Wholesale Club, and other wholesalers and retailers, including supermarkets, supercenters, internet retailers, gasoline stations, hard discounters, department stores, and specialty stores. The company values its intellectual property, including trademarks, trade names, copyrights, proprietary processes, trade secrets, trade dress, and domain names, particularly its Costco Wholesale and Kirkland Signature brands, which it believes offer high quality at lower prices than national brands and contribute to higher margins. Kirkland Signature products represent a growing portion of sales and are expected to see increased sales penetration. The company protects its intellectual property through trademark and copyright laws, trade-secret protection, and confidentiality, license, and other agreements with suppliers, employees, and others. Trademark registrations vary by country but are generally valid and renewable indefinitely as long as in use and maintained. Costco’s U.S. website is www.costco.com, where it provides free access to Annual Reports on Form 10-K, Quarterly Reports on Form 10-Q, Current Reports on Form 8-K, Proxy Statements, and Forms 3, 4, and 5, as well as amendments, as soon as reasonably practicable after filing with the SEC. Information on the website is not part of the Annual Report. The SEC’s website (www.sec.gov) contains reports and other information about issuers. Costco has adopted a code of ethics for senior financial officers under Section 406 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, and copies are available by writing to Secretary, Costco Wholesale Corporation, 999 Lake Drive, Issaquah, WA 98027. Any amendments to the code (excluding technical, administrative, or non-substantive ones) or waivers to the CEO, CFO, or principal accounting officer and controller are disclosed on the website or in a Form 8-K filing with the SEC. Key business risks include heavy dependence on U.S. and Canadian operations, which accounted for 86% and 81% of net sales and operating income in 2021, respectively, with California representing 28% of U.S. net sales and having a higher concentration of high-volume warehouses. Declines in performance in these areas could result from slow growth, rising labor, healthcare, and energy costs, failure to meet warehouse opening targets, cannibalization of existing locations, shifts in sales mix toward lower-margin products, economic downturns, or failure to deliver quality products. Growth depends on acquiring property and building or leasing new warehouses, which faces challenges from land use regulations, community opposition, and local laws restricting operations or expansion. New warehouse openings may draw members away from existing locations and negatively affect comparable sales, traffic, and profitability. Expanding into new markets involves risks such as lack of brand familiarity, difficulty attracting members, seasonal differences, and competition from established players. Investments in supply chain and delivery efficiency may not deliver expected benefits or returns. Failure to maintain membership growth, loyalty, and brand recognition could harm profitability. The Kirkland Signature brand is essential for member loyalty, with consistent quality, pricing, and availability critical to maintaining trust and higher margins. Disruptions in distribution, processing, packaging, manufacturing, or other facilities due to natural disasters, pandemics, labor issues, or shipping problems could delay deliveries and reduce member satisfaction. The e-commerce business relies on third-party and in-house logistics providers, whose service disruptions negatively impact operations. Failure to identify or respond to consumer trends could reduce demand, harm relationships, and affect market share. Inaccurate sales forecasting may lead to excess inventory or stockouts, increasing markdowns or delivery delays and reducing operating performance. The company’s information technology systems are vital for processing transactions, inventory tracking, and decision-making; disruptions or failures in these systems could impair operations, including inability to purchase from suppliers, produce goods, or deliver products. Ongoing IT transformation projects are critical, and failure to execute them efficiently could result in loss of competitive position and harm to financial condition and results. The company is investing in digital resiliency to prevent disruptions from power outages, cyberattacks, security breaches, employee errors, or catastrophic events, and any failure of critical IT systems or data centers would require significant recovery efforts and could severely impact business operations.

To buy products and services from suppliers, produce goods in manufacturing plants, move products efficiently to warehouses, and sell to members, the company is undertaking large technology and IT transformation projects. The failure of these projects could negatively impact business plans and impair daily operations. Given the high volume of transactions, strong digital resiliency is essential to prevent disruptions from power outages, computer or telecommunications failures, viruses, internal or external security breaches, employee errors, and catastrophic events like fires, earthquakes, tornadoes, or hurricanes. A significant failure in critical IT systems, data centers, or backup systems would require substantial resources to restore services and could severely disrupt business operations, including loss of services, increased costs to move merchandise, and failure to serve members. The company is making substantial investments to maintain and enhance digital resiliency; delays or failures in these efforts could be costly and harmful. Inefficient or ineffective delivery of IT transformation could result in loss of competitive advantage and adverse effects on financial condition and operations. The company must maintain the privacy and security of personal and business information amid growing threats and comply with global privacy and data protection regulations, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, California Consumer Privacy Act, and Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. Failure to do so could damage its reputation with members, suppliers, and employees, lead to substantial costs, and result in litigation or regulatory action. Increased and more sophisticated cyber threats, including phishing attacks that serve as vectors for ransomware, pose risks to systems, networks, and data. The company relies on IT systems and networks—some managed by third parties—for all business activities and processes sensitive information about members, suppliers, and employees. Remote work due to the COVID-19 pandemic has expanded attack surfaces, and threats to gain unauthorized access are becoming more frequent and sophisticated. Cybersecurity attacks can range from random attempts to targeted, coordinated actions, including advanced persistent threats. While employees are trained, that training is not fully effective, and vulnerabilities in IT systems or third-party managed systems (such as cloud providers) may go unnoticed. Despite cybersecurity and compliance efforts, there is no guarantee that current or future controls will fully protect systems, information, or property. A material cybersecurity attack could lead to reputational damage, litigation, government enforcement, penalties, system disruptions, unauthorized data release, data corruption, reduced value of IT investments, and higher remediation costs—adversely affecting competitiveness, operations, financial condition, and, critically, member confidence. Insurance coverage and third-party indemnification may be insufficient to cover claims, costs, or liabilities. The company is subject to payment-related risks, accepting payments via credit and debit cards, cash, checks, co-brand rebates, Executive member 2% reward certificates, and shop cards. As new payment options are introduced, additional rules, compliance requirements, and higher fraud losses may arise. The company relies on third parties for credit and debit card and shop card transaction processing; disruptions from these parties could impact operations. It is also subject to evolving rules from payment card associations, including Payment Card Industry Data Security Standards, which require security measures for the physical and electronic storage, processing, and transmission of cardholder data. A breach of internal systems could result in liability for card re-issuance, fines, higher transaction fees, loss of card acceptance, and negative impacts on business and operations. The sale of products—including food, drugs, children’s products, pet products, and durable goods—carries risks of illness or injury due to tampering, contamination, spoilage, foreign objects, faulty design, or other issues. Suppliers are contractually required to comply with safety laws, and the company depends on them to meet safety and standards. Despite governmental inspections and compliance efforts, illness or injury from products could lead to lost sales, increased costs, litigation, or reputational harm. Even if claims are unsuccessful, negative publicity could harm the company’s reputation and brand image long-term. Failure to develop and maintain a relevant omnichannel experience—such as mobile apps and websites—could adversely affect results, as members increasingly use digital devices and social media to shop, especially post-COVID-19. The company is investing in these platforms, but failure to timely improve or develop them could harm competitiveness and operations. Inability to attract, train, and retain qualified employees—especially senior management and key operations, IT, merchandising, and administrative staff—could negatively impact business, financial condition, and operations. Success depends on employee contributions, and without a succession plan for senior management, business performance could suffer. The company competes for talent amid rising labor costs, regulatory changes, healthcare expenses, and wage rates, and there is no assurance of future success in attracting or retaining qualified personnel. Claims for health benefits, workers’ compensation, general liability, property damage, directors’ and officers’ liability, vehicle liability, inventory loss, and other exposures are primarily self-insured, with limited insurance for large losses. Significant claims, regulatory changes, rising healthcare or insurance costs, or failure to maintain adequate coverage could harm financial condition and operations. Although specific coverages exist for catastrophic property losses, the company still bears a significant portion of the risk from physical damage to warehouses, depots, manufacturing or home office facilities, inventory loss or spoilage, and business interruption—potentially impacting cash flows and operations. The company faces strong competition from other retailers and warehouse club operators, including supermarkets, supercenters, internet retailers, gasoline stations, hard discounters, department stores, and specialty operators, who compete on pricing, selection, services, location, convenience, and digital experience. The evolution of online and mobile retail has intensified competition, with some competitors having greater financial resources, technology, access to merchandise, and market penetration. Inability to respond to competitive pressures or changing customer expectations could result in lost market share and negative financial results. General economic factors—such as higher energy and gasoline costs, inflation, unemployment, healthcare costs, consumer debt, foreign exchange rates, unsettled financial markets, housing market weaknesses, reduced consumer confidence, changes in tax policies, sovereign debt crises, pandemics, and other economic factors—could reduce demand, require product mix changes, or increase inventory costs. Actions in countries like China, the United States, and the United Kingdom have raised costs and created uncertainty about tariffs, which affect merchandise pricing and margins. The impact depends on product types, tariff rates, and timing. Fluctuations in commodity prices—such as gasoline and consumable goods—due to supply and demand, inflation, labor costs, competition, speculation, regulations, taxes, and delivery delays can affect sales, profit margins, and operating expenses. Inflation in merchandise costs may reduce profitability if prices cannot be adjusted without hurting consumer demand. Certain categories have seen inflation beyond recent trends due to pandemic and economic uncertainty. Suppliers may fail to deliver quality merchandise in sufficient quantities at competitive prices or may not meet quality, packaging, legal, regulatory, labor, environmental, or animal welfare standards, leading to inventory issues, lost sales, and profit margin declines. The company depends on purchasing quality merchandise in large volumes at competitive prices, but there is no assurance of continued supply, pricing, or access to new products. Suppliers can change terms or discontinue sales, and member demand may lead to out-of-stock situations. The company buys from numerous domestic and foreign manufacturers and importers; loss of key suppliers or inability to develop new relationships could harm operations. Products from alternative sources may be lower quality or more expensive. High quality standards, especially for food items, may limit supply, making consistent availability difficult. Suppliers face risks such as labor disputes, union activities, financial instability, natural disasters, extreme weather, public health emergencies, supply constraints, and economic or political conditions that could delay or prevent timely delivery. Deficiencies in quality or compliance may go undetected before products are sold, leading to recalls, litigation, reputational damage, increased costs, and negative impacts on business. Fluctuations in foreign exchange rates may negatively affect results, as international operations—including Canada—accounted for 28% of net sales and 36% of operating income in 2021, and the company plans to grow internationally. Financial statements are translated from local currencies to U.S. dollars using current exchange rates. Unfavorable exchange rate fluctuations could harm Canadian and other international operations and negatively affect period-over-period results. A portion of purchased products is paid for in a currency different from the local sale currency, so currency fluctuations may increase merchandise costs and prevent those costs from being passed on to members, adversely affecting operations. Natural disasters, extreme weather, public health emergencies, or other catastrophic events—such as hurricanes, floods, earthquakes, wildfires, droughts, terrorism, energy shortages, or pandemics—could damage property, limit store hours, reduce member visits, temporarily close facilities, disrupt IT systems, delay deliveries, or reduce product availability. These events could also disrupt supplier or member operations, reduce consumer spending, and lower demand. The company may be required to suspend operations, which could materially harm business, financial condition, and results. The ongoing impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic continue to affect operations, demand, in-stock positions, costs, labor availability, inventory access, supply chain operations, performance forecasting, exposure to litigation, and financial performance. The pandemic has had widespread effects on the global economy and on employees, members, suppliers, and other business partners. Uncertainty remains about the virus’s spread and the duration of containment measures such as travel bans, quarantines, shelter-in-place orders, and business shutdowns. These actions may cause business disruption, reduced member traffic, lower sales in certain categories, and higher operating expenses. The pandemic has disrupted global supply chains due to business restrictions, straining domestic and international supply chains and potentially continuing to affect product availability. Member demand for certain products has fluctuated as behaviors change, challenging inventory forecasting and adjustment. Increased online purchases have strained fulfillment operations, causing delivery delays and lost sales from out-of-stock SKUs. Failure to appropriately respond—or the perception of an inadequate response—could have adverse consequences.

The pandemic continues to create significant uncertainty regarding the spread of COVID-19 and the duration and scope of containment measures such as travel bans, quarantines, shelter-in-place orders, and business or government shutdowns. These measures, along with actions taken by governments or the company itself, may lead to business disruptions, reduced member traffic, lower sales in certain merchandise categories, and increased operating expenses. The global supply chain remains disrupted due to restrictions on business activities, straining both domestic and international supply chains and potentially reducing the availability of certain products. Member demand for specific products has fluctuated and may continue to do so as pandemic-related behaviors evolve, challenging the company’s ability to forecast and adjust inventory levels. Increased online purchasing has placed pressure on fulfillment operations, resulting in delivery delays and lost sales from stockouts of certain SKUs. A failure to adequately respond to evolving pandemic conditions—or a perception of such a failure—could damage the company’s brand, lead to lost sales, and result in claims from employees, members, suppliers, regulators, or other parties. A future outbreak of confirmed COVID-19 cases in company facilities could cause temporary or long-term workforce shortages or facility closures, negatively impacting operations. Some jurisdictions have introduced measures to expand workers’ compensation availability or alter presumptions, which may increase claims and costs. Other key uncertainties include the severity and duration of the pandemic, future virus variants, evolving macroeconomic factors like unemployment and recession, changes in labor markets, the impact of time and resources invested in pandemic response, the pace of economic recovery, long-term shifts in consumer behavior, and financial market volatility. Continued adverse effects of the pandemic on the U.S. and global economy could amplify existing risks, such as consumer expectations, competition, brand reputation, cybersecurity, payment risks, technology disruptions, supply chain issues, labor availability and cost, litigation, and operational risks from remote work. Climate change risks also affect operations, as the company uses natural gas, diesel, gasoline, and electricity in distribution and warehouse activities. Government regulations limiting greenhouse gas emissions may raise compliance and merchandise costs, while energy input regulations could materially affect profitability. Climate-related events such as extreme weather, wildfires, droughts, and rising sea levels could disrupt the procurement of commodities at current cost and volume levels. The company sells a substantial amount of gasoline, whose demand may be affected by climate concerns and increasing regulation. Failure to meet financial market expectations—such as warehouse and e-commerce comparable sales growth, membership renewal rates, new member sign-ups, gross margin, earnings, earnings per share, new warehouse openings, or dividend and stock repurchase policies—could cause a decline in the stock price. The company is subject to legal, regulatory, accounting, political, and economic risks in the regions where it operates, including political and economic instability, regulatory constraints, currency regulations, policy changes like the U.K.’s withdrawal from the EU, trade barriers, monetary and fiscal policies, and difficulties in enforcing intellectual property rights. Changes in accounting standards or management’s subjective assumptions, estimates, and judgments related to complex accounting matters—such as self-insurance liabilities—could significantly affect financial performance and consolidated financial statements. The company is exposed to risks under Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, which requires management assessments of internal control effectiveness; failure to maintain effective controls could impair financial reporting, lead to litigation or investigations, erode investor confidence, and negatively impact the stock price. Changes in tax rates, new U.S. or foreign tax laws, or additional tax liabilities could harm financial condition and results. The company is subject to various taxes and tax obligations in the U.S. and foreign jurisdictions and may be under examination for value-added, sales, payroll, product, import, or other taxes. Changes in tax laws, administrative practices, or interpretations could result in additional tax expenses, liabilities, or penalties, and changes in enacted tax rates or adverse audit outcomes—such as transfer pricing disputes—could materially affect financial results. The company faces environmental risks related to the use, storage, discharge, and disposal of hazardous materials and wastes, with non-compliance potentially leading to harm to members or employees, significant remediation costs, penalties, or operational restrictions. Operations at facilities involve wastewater, stormwater, and agricultural or food processing waste management, refrigeration systems (including ammonia-based chillers), noise, odor, and dust control, and mechanized equipment, all of which may impact public health and the environment. Failure to meet environmental, health, and safety standards could result in fines, employee illness or injury, lawsuits, and temporary facility closures. The company is involved in various legal proceedings and audits, including grand jury and government investigations, consumer, employment, tort, and unclaimed property claims, and other litigation. Outcomes of these proceedings are unpredictable and could require actions that negatively affect operations or result in substantial payments, harming financial condition and results. Defending these matters may involve significant expenses and divert management attention and resources. At the end of 2021, the company operated 251 warehouses outside the U.S. and planned to continue expanding international operations. International results could be negatively affected by political and economic conditions, regulatory constraints, currency regulations, policy changes, foreign trade (including tariffs and sanctions), monetary and fiscal policies, U.S. and foreign laws, and risks associated with facilities in less stable regions. International operations also face challenges such as high management costs, adverse tax consequences, and difficulty enforcing intellectual property rights. As of August 29, 2021, the company operated 815 membership warehouses: 454 in the U.S. and Puerto Rico, 89 in Canada, and 101 in other international regions, with 121 of the 171 leases being land-only leases where Costco owns the building. The warehouses contained approximately 118.9 million square feet of operating floor space—83.2 million in the U.S., 14.9 million in Canada, and 20.8 million in other international regions—and about 31.4 million square feet in distribution and logistics facilities. The company also operates processing, packaging, manufacturing, and other facilities to produce private-label items. The company’s common stock is traded on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the symbol “COST.” As of September 28, 2021, there were 9,958 stockholders of record. Dividends are declared by the Board of Directors and are based on profitability and expected capital needs, with the company currently planning to pay dividends quarterly. The company’s common stock repurchase program, authorized in April 2019 for $4,000 and expiring in April 2023, totaled 318,000 shares in the fourth quarter of 2021, with an average price paid of $398.76 per share. In 2021, the company combined hardlines and softlines into a non-foods category, a change that did not materially affect results of operations. The company defines comparable sales as net sales from warehouses open for more than one year, including remodels, relocations, expansions, and e-commerce sites open for more than one year. Comparable sales growth is driven by increased shopping frequency and average ticket size from new and existing members. Sales are influenced by factors beyond the company’s control, such as currency exchange rates and changes in gasoline prices and competitive conditions. Higher comparable sales growth, excluding these factors, allows for a reduction in selling, general, and administrative (SG&A) expenses as a percentage of sales, improving profitability. Net sales growth is also influenced by the health of the economies in which the company operates, including inflation or deflation, particularly in the U.S. Net sales and gross margins are affected by strong competition from global, national, and regional wholesalers and retailers, including those with e-commerce operations.

Net sales increased 18% to $192,052 in 2021, driven by a 16% increase in comparable sales and sales from new warehouses opened in 2020 and 2021. Comparable sales grew 16%, resulting from higher shopping frequency and increased average ticket, with e-commerce comparable sales rising 44% in 2021, including an 80% increase in the first half of the year. Sales in non-foods and warehouse ancillary and other businesses, such as e-commerce and gasoline, were particularly strong. Net sales growth was also influenced by changes in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar, which positively impacted net sales by $2,759 or 169 basis points, and by a 12% increase in the average price per gallon of gasoline, which added $1,636 or 100 basis points, along with a $1,469 or 90 basis point boost from a 10% volume increase in gasoline sales. The total gross margin percentage decreased seven basis points to 11.13%, primarily due to a shift in sales penetration toward warehouse ancillary and other businesses; however, excluding the impact of gasoline price inflation, gross margin percentage improved to 11.22%, up two basis points, driven by better performance in core merchandise categories, especially non-foods, and in warehouse ancillary and other businesses, as well as a three basis point positive impact from a 2020 inventory reserve that was not recorded in 2021. This was partially offset by a two basis point LIFO charge and a 2% increase in rewards. SG&A expenses as a percentage of net sales decreased 40 basis points to 9.61%, mainly due to leveraging increased sales and lower incremental wages related to COVID-19, with warehouse operations and other businesses contributing a 24 basis point reduction, while central operating costs, stock compensation, and acquisition-related costs also declined. Preopening expenses were $76 in 2021, compared to $55 in 2020, with a total of 22 warehouse openings and relocations, including 12 net new in the U.S., 4 in Canada, and 4 in Other International, compared to 16 in 2020. Membership fees increased 9% to $3,877, driven by sign-ups and upgrades to Executive membership, with renewal rates of 91% in the U.S. and Canada and 89% worldwide, and excluding foreign currency impacts, membership fees grew 8%. Note 1—Summary of Significant Accounting Policies  
Description of Business  
Costco Wholesale Corporation (Costco or the Company), a Washington corporation, and its subsidiaries operate membership warehouses based on the concept that offering members low prices on a limited selection of nationally-branded and private-label products in a wide range of merchandise categories will produce high sales volumes and rapid inventory turnover. At August 29, 2021, Costco operated 815 warehouses worldwide: 564 in the United States (U.S.) located in 46 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, 105 in Canada, 39 in Mexico, 30 in Japan, 29 in the United Kingdom (U.K.), 16 in Korea, 14 in Taiwan, 12 in Australia, three in Spain, and one each in Iceland, France and China. The Company operates e-commerce websites in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Mexico, Korea, Taiwan, Japan, and Australia.  
Basis of Presentation  
The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of Costco, its wholly-owned subsidiaries, and subsidiaries in which it has a controlling interest. The Company reports noncontrolling interests in consolidated entities as a component of equity separate from the Company’s equity. All material inter-company transactions between and among the Company and its consolidated subsidiaries have been eliminated in consolidation. The Company’s net income excludes income attributable to the noncontrolling interest in Taiwan. Unless otherwise noted, references to net income relate to net income attributable to Costco.  
Fiscal Year End  
The Company operates on a 52/53-week fiscal year basis with the year ending on the Sunday closest to August 31. References to 2021, 2020, and 2019 relate to the 52-week fiscal years ended August 29, 2021, August 30, 2020, and September 1, 2019, respectively.  
Use of Estimates  
The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles (U.S. GAAP) requires management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities and the disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. These estimates and assumptions take into account historical and forward-looking factors that the Company believes are reasonable, including but not limited to the potential impacts arising from the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) and related public and private sector policies and initiatives. Actual results could differ from those estimates and assumptions.  
Cash and Cash Equivalents  
The Company considers as cash and cash equivalents all cash on deposit, highly liquid investments with a maturity of three months or less at the date of purchase, and proceeds due from credit and debit card transactions with settlement terms of up to four days. Credit and debit card receivables were $1,816 and $1,636 at the end of 2021 and 2020, respectively.

Short-Term Investments  
Short-term investments generally consist of debt securities (U.S. Government and Agency Notes), with maturities at the date of purchase of three months to five years. Investments with maturities beyond five years may be classified, based on the Company’s determination, as short-term based on their highly liquid nature and because they represent the investment of cash that is available for current operations. Short-term investments classified as available-for-sale are recorded at fair value using the specific identification method with the unrealized gains and losses reflected in accumulated other comprehensive income (loss) until realized. Realized gains and losses from the sale of available-for-sale securities, if any, are determined on a specific identification basis and are recorded in interest income and other, net in the consolidated statements of income. These available-for-sale investments have a low level of inherent credit risk given they are issued by the U.S. Government and Agencies. Changes in their fair value are primarily attributable to changes in interest rates and market liquidity. Short-term investments classified as held-to-maturity are financial instruments that the Company has the intent and ability to hold to maturity and are reported net of any related amortization and are not remeasured to fair value on a recurring basis.  
The Company periodically evaluates unrealized losses in its investment securities for credit impairment, using both qualitative and quantitative criteria. In the event a security is deemed to be impaired as the result of a credit loss, the Company recognizes the loss in interest income and other, net in the consolidated statements of income.  
Fair Value of Financial Instruments  
The Company accounts for certain assets and liabilities at fair value. The carrying value of the Company’s financial instruments, including cash and cash equivalents, receivables and accounts payable, approximate fair value due to their short-term nature or variable interest rates. See Notes 3, 4, and 5 for the carrying value and fair value of the Company’s investments, derivative instruments, and fixed-rate debt, respectively.  
Fair value is defined as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. Fair value is estimated by applying a fair value hierarchy, which requires maximizing the use of observable inputs when measuring fair value. The three levels of inputs are:  
Level 1: Quoted market prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.  
Level 2: Observable market-based inputs or unobservable inputs that are corroborated by market data.  
Level 3: Significant unobservable inputs that are not corroborated by market data.  
The Company’s valuation techniques used to measure the fair value of money market mutual funds are based on quoted market prices, such as quoted net asset values published by the fund as supported in an active market. Valuation methodologies used to measure the fair value of all other non-derivative financial instruments are based on independent external valuation information. The pricing process uses data from a variety of independent external valuation information providers, including trades, bid price or spread, two-sided markets, quotes, benchmark curves including but not limited to treasury benchmarks and LIBOR or Secured Overnight Financing Rate and swap curves, discount rates, and market data feeds. All are observable in the market or can be derived principally from or corroborated by observable market data. The Company reports transfers in and out of Levels 1, 2, and 3, as applicable, using the fair value of the individual securities as of the beginning of the reporting period in which the transfer(s) occurred.  
Current financial liabilities have fair values that approximate their carrying values. Long-term financial liabilities include the Company's long-term debt, which are recorded on the balance sheet at issuance price and adjusted for unamortized discounts or premiums and debt issuance costs, and are being amortized to interest expense over the term of the loan. The estimated fair value of the Company's long-term debt is based primarily on reported market values, recently completed market transactions, and estimates based upon interest rates, maturities, and credit.  
Receivables, Net  
Receivables consist primarily of vendor, reinsurance, credit card incentive, third-party pharmacy and other receivables. Vendor receivables include discounts and volume rebates. Balances are generally presented on a gross basis, separate from any related payable due. In certain circumstances, these receivables may be settled against the related payable to that vendor, in which case the receivables are presented on a net basis. Reinsurance receivables are held by the Company’s wholly-owned captive insurance subsidiary and primarily represent amounts ceded through reinsurance arrangements gross of the amounts assumed under reinsurance, which are presented within other current liabilities in the consolidated balance sheets. Credit card incentive receivables primarily represent amounts earned under the co-branded credit card arrangement in the U.S. Third-party pharmacy receivables generally relate to amounts due from members’ insurers. Other receivables primarily consist of amounts due from governmental entities, mostly tax-related items.  
Receivables are recorded net of an allowance for credit losses which considers creditworthiness of vendors and third parties, historical experience and current economic trends. Write-offs of receivables were immaterial in 2021, 2020, and 2019.
